title: Prayers for peace in afterlife
article: Long Duy Hoang lived dangerously and died violently, but his daybreak send-off Tuesday was filled with wishes for a peaceful afterlife.
Hoang, 28, known on the street as Crazy Jimmy, was in an open casket at the front of the funeral chapel, his forehead wrapped in a scarf and his chest covered in freshly cut flowers.
Mourners in black suits and platform shoes streamed into the service, bringing flowers and consoling the Hoang family.

A shrine to Hoang was erected at the front of the chapel, containing a youthful picture of him, vibrant and smiling, as well as traditional foods and tea, a carton of cigarettes, candles and incense to guide and sustain him on his way to the next world. Next to it was a second shrine to Buddha.

Hoang died of multiple gunshot wounds Jan. 7 after a shoot-out two days earlier with Edmonton police. Police said Hoang was a known enforcer in one of two local gangs battling over the city's drug trade. Many of the gang leaders are of Vietnamese descent.
But the signs of Hoang's violent demise were absent Tuesday, save for a few purple bruises and a pinched expression that showed through the dead man's heavy face makeup.

The hour-long ceremony, conducted in Vietnamese, drew about 40 people, mostly young men of Asian ancestry. A friend said Hoang's parents couldn't make the trip from Vietnam but aunts and uncles were present.

Just prior to the ceremony, one man gathered a handful of younger men from the crowd and motioned for them to sit in the front row, across the aisle from the Hoang family. They squeezed into the pew, eight abreast.
Then Hoang's siblings knelt at the foot of the shrines as monks sang and chanted.

When the ceremony was over, a family friend thanked everyone for coming, then beckoned people forward to say a few words. A friend of Hoang's parents made a brief statement and, as he was concluding, a cellular phone at the back of the chapel rang more than a dozen times, drawing stern glances.
The criminal investigation into events leading up to and following Hoang's death is continuing.

When that is completed -- it could take weeks or months -- a use- of-force review board will be convened to examine whether police discharged firearms in accordance with the law and police policy. It is not a public process.
The board will submit its findings to Police Chief John Lindsay, who may ask for a review by the staff sergeant in charge of internal affairs.
That, too, is an internal process.
Later in the year, when police investigations are completed, a provincial court judge will conduct a public fatality inquiry to determine what happened and whether it could have been avoided.
Police were acting on two anonymous tips when they tracked a Honda Accord to a west-end home Jan. 5 and chased the vehicle when it left the house about 8 p.m.

Police say the Honda crashed into a parked Jeep minutes later. The passenger, Hoa Tran, surrendered. The driver, Hoang, allegedly fired a handgun at police, prompting three of six officers to return fire.
